comments.text: How did it age badly? 24GB is still not even close to being required for gaming. This also relates in no way to the issue we have with 8GB GPUs, so it's a ridiculous comparison to make.

comments.text:
​ @Hardwareunboxed  Because 10GB on the 3080 was an actual scam by nvidia, as well as some of the later victims of VRAM-gouging, like most 4070 models only having 12GB or the 5080 being handicapped by 16GB.
A $750 upper mid-ranger like the 5070 ti having 16GB is fine, but the 5080 should've never shipped with only 16GB. It already fails to run Indy at max settings with PT. As in it literally cannot run it, from what I am aware, as Indy with max everything required 20GB minimum or else it just crashes.
The 5080 is the like.. 3rd or 4th fastest? consumer-grade GPU and it cannot even run a game from 2024 fully maxed out. And that, like you guys keep screeching about with 8/etc GB cards, will become a more prevalent issue down the road for the 5080 with its, honestly measly, 16GB of VRAM. A high-end GPU that can't really do high-end gaming, solely because of its VRAM buffer.

24GB was overkill in 2020. Even for 4k. FF to just 23/24/25 and 24GB is what all high-end cards should've shipped with from the get-go. Instead people got scammed with the 5080 16GB and now the Super with 24GB will release rather soon, being the GPU that the base 5080 should've been, both in core count and VRAM.

I own a 3080 10GB and I bought a 3090 a few days ago. Solely because the 10GB buffer isn't enough, especially with multiple things open. It's an actual shame these cards got screwed.
Go ahead and try it yourself. Run a 3080 10GB with triple screens and a couple dozen browser tabs open. Shit will slow to a crawl, especially the longer Firefox stays open the more RAM and VRAM it will hog. While it does seem to an a known issue with FF specifically, not releasing VRAM resources properly, it just adds on everything else, not being able to run games at max settings. Like again.. 5080 running Indy maxed out? It can't. 3080 10GB running RE4 maxed out with RT? It can't, you'll also just crash unless you put textures below 4GB and/or mess with shadow settings. And texture settings at max will actually run fine otherwise. You can do 8 or whatever GB textures in RE4. As far as I am aware nothing fails to load, and you avoid the ugly mis-match that's present with lower texture settings. On consoles textures of all objects match each other's resolution, while on PC you can run 3-4GB textures and have higher-than-console textures on most objects, while some pile of clothes or rubbish on the ground's super blurry for some reason. And that's because Capcom doesn't care about their games on PC. That's why their engine issues with TAA were never resolved, why RE4's RT VRAM crashing was never resolved, and why 10GB on the 3080 was a really dumb move by nvidia, and with 16GB on the 5080 will 100% handicap it in the future, and you can screenshot this comment and print it out and hang it up somewhere to remind you that eventually I'll be right. The 5080 16GB will run into limitations more frequently in 2026/27, and by 2028 that card will be severely handicapped at 4k high/max settings with upscaling, especially once FG comes into the mix.
comments.author: @imaginarymenageriemanager6303

comments.text: How does any of this relate to the 24GB cards you're commenting on? Saying 24GB is overkill on the 3090 isn't somehow justifying 10GB on the 3080. What sort of mental gymnastics are you playing at here?
comments.author: @Hardwareunboxed

comments.text:
@Hardwareunboxed  Because 24GB is actually adequate for the 3090. Whether it's a Titan or just the highest "gaming" tier GPU like what the 1080 ti was back in the day. 24GB for the 3090 wasn't overkill, it was adequate, adequate for the price tag and the tier of hardware it was in. What wasn't adequate at all was 10GB on the 3080, 8GB on the 3070 and the other atrocities I've mentioned, like most 4070 models only having 12GB or the 5080, a high-end $1400 at launch GPU only having 16GB as well.
24GB on this card was genuinely a good move and it benefited "gamers" in the long-run as much as it benefited professionals from day one.
If anything you should make a video about this card and how it's holding up right now, especially in comparison to the 3080/ti. Back then these cards were neck on neck, but as I've said that changed in only just 2~ years after launch. 2022/23 is when more and more very VRAM demanding games and technologies released/become more prevalent.
The 3090 can't do DLSS FG sadly, but it still has FSR FG and whatever else's floating around like "Lossless"Scaling.
Its core is still very good, it has a very high bandwidth at almost a TB/s and you have plenty of actual memory too. I mean you could argue, which some people do, that the base 3080's bandwidth is super high too and that helps it a lot, which is totally true, but that only goes so far. Bandwidth isn't everything and neither is the actual memory amount, as well as the type of memory used and hell, the lanes. I mean nvidia releasing x8 GPUs is a different topic.

I'd genuinely like to see a comparison video between the base 3080, either the 12GB model or the 3080 ti, and the 3090.
These cards were all 4k cards back then and right now can still do 4k natively/with upscaling, depending on the game.
A video specifically for 4k native and with upscaling, as well as with RT on/off and with FG via FSR whenever supported.

I have no doubt in my mind that the 3080 will struggle a lot more than the 12GB mode/ti, and the 3090 will still have zero issues. Again, the 3090 can do Indy max settings PT, whereas sub-20GB GPUs can't. 4k DLSS IIRC*
Or the 3060 12GB model being able to run RE4 at max settings with RT above 30fps at all times @ 1440p, while the 3070 literally cannot do it. THe 3070 will simply crash. The 3080 will simply crash. It required more than 10GB to run RE4 at max settings RT @ 1440p, actually just 1080p. I can't do it on my 10GB card, I'll crash too. It's just the fact the 3060 12GB can actually do 1440p playable above 30fps max everything, while the 3070 simply can't.

You may seem this as a ramble or incoherent rant, but it's no more incoherent than you guys' podcasts when you're going off tangent.

Do a video and prove me wrong. Now more than ever is the time to actually discuss VRAM and show people how much nvidia screwed people with these cards. 30 series and both the 40 and 50 series cards, 4070 models and the 5080 will run into these same issues down the road as well, actually worse since these cards support FG via DLSS and FG is becoming more and more a requirement sadly. How well do you think is a 5080 16GB holding up at 4k max everything (with/without upscaling) just a good year from now, beginning of 2027? By then it'll be 2 years old and already start to struggle more. Now imagine it another 2 years in 2029. 4 years was perfectly fine for a high-end GPU in the past, now you're screwed unless you specifically go for high VRAM cards.
And the reason, two reasons, why I don't consider the 4080 having been screwed are 1. it was released in 2022, 3 years ago (and not 7-8 months ago) and 2. it only supports 2x FG via DLSS.
It really sucks that it can't do 3-4x FG too, but it's another factor to consider. A $1000-1400 GPU releasing in 2022 with 16GB? Fine, still good, adequate.
A $1000-1400 GPU (basically the same one, just a refresh with slightly better software features) releasing in 2025 with still 16GB? Not okay, not when it's supposed to last someone 4-5 years at the minimum.

comments.text:
It's so unfortunate to see NVIDIA market this card so poorly. Based on the hardware specs and the recent analogy to the Titan series, this card is obviously built for processing jobs (media, data science, AI, etc.). I bought the 3090 Ti this week, knowing full well this is a purchase for my research rig. The next step up is the RTX A5000 at $3100 and it does not have a serious performance boost over the 3090 on AI benchmarks, making the 3090 Ti the clear choice in my use case. 

But, there is still an argument to be made for gaming here considering the current market. You can still find 3080s and 3090s going for $2000. Depending on how hard someone is looking and how long they want to look for, a 3090 Ti makes sense from a money point, if you have money: if I'm spending $1.5-2K on a GPU, might as well be the "best" one ("best" being vague here). 

Still, I agree with the point: 3090 Ti is a weird move from NVIDIA and a totally lackluster response, if not insulting, to the current gaming GPU market.

With 450W on the GPU and 240W on the CPU, system power draw needs to include the power cost of air conditioning the rooms these systems exist in.
With just over 700W on a Ryzen Test system, you could bump that up to 800W for an Intel 12900K based system. With aircon cooling you get roughly 3:1 cooling power to power draw, so that 700-800W system power draw is actually over a kilowatt if you want to maintain your ambient room temperatures.

Of course you get that power benefit using it as a heater in winter, with varying power benefits of ~30% vs aircon to 100% vs radiator.

comments.text: After owning a RTX 3080 factory OC model that consumes about 340w since launchday, I can wholeheartedly say that my next upgrade will be from the manufacturer that offers the best performance PER WATT at around 300w max. I went from a GPU that used about 200w to 340w. That is a 140w increase. In my very well ventilated case, this meant that overall temps went up significantly. Noise also went up just as much. My CPU, chipset and memory temps went up noticeably as well. This is in case with 2x 140mm fans, 3x 120mm fans and 1x 160mm fan as case fans, and 2x 140mm CPU fans. All BeQuiet! Silent Wings 3 fans. I also noticed the much warmer overall temperature in the room, and PC gaming all of a sudden started to get uncomfortably warm and sweaty on warm days. No way will I purchase a card that generates even more heat. It's just not an option. Energy prices are also rapidly increasing all over Europe thanks to the ongoing war, several hundred percent increase in some countries just in the last month. At that point I will rather play games on my PS5, which consumes about 215w MAX in total for the entire box! Do I appreciate 120+fps? Yes. Is it worth consuming upwards of 1000w in total versus a console at 215w for 60fps? NOPE.

comments.text:
@solocamo3654  Percentages in clarity means nothing without an expected viewing distance. And once the pixels become smaller than what you can individually detect the word "clarity" loses it's meaning and should be substituted with something that conveys that it's a scientific measurement.

I think a Ferrari Enzo is also a stupid vehicle. Sure, it is better in some technical merits, that I get to pay a premium for, which solves a set of problems I don't have. This is where I'm coming from with the "4k is stupid" remark. No, I can't just go to 1080p or 720p by that same reductionist logic. Because those resolutions look noticeably worse. They look "pixely" to me. 1440p doesn't. And I'm a programmer. I look at my screen all day long. Especially for well anti aliased text there is no practical difference. Sure it may be "better" in some objective sense but if it doesn't look better I get no benefit... Now if you happen to sit with your nose against a huge monitor, sure, you may value the difference. But man do you get to pay for it. A +170Hz 4K monitor doesn't come cheap (are there even any out yet?) and getting a proper 90FPS experience without DLSS or dialling down settings in every '22 AAA title isn't even possible. But if this clarity thing matters more to you than silky smooth scrolling and fast games... well I guess it's not stupid to you. Just like the Ferrari Enzo isn't stupid to everyone (I mean, they do manage to sell the things after all).

Most of that card's bulk is the cooling element, just like always.  People who don't regularly take their cards apart don't notice that.  Most video card boards are pretty small/thin .. with a massive heat plate covering it and then a bulky heat pipe / fin design with 1-3 small fans.

There are some elements of design that can make your radiator more efficient, which is how 3rd party custom coolers make their money. But generally speaking, if you want to have more cooling, you just have more metal attached to it and more airflow.  It's not really an engineering marvel, it's 100 year old tech.

for every bad AMD driver, Nvidia tends to have the same issues
